title: A stopping voltage is a magnitude with a sign convention
question: Why does retarding an electron not make its charge positive?
recap: The ideal stopping-potential magnitude is Kmax divided by the positive elementary-charge magnitude. Partial transfer or internal losses produce an inequality rather than a larger endpoint energy.
premises: e denotes a positive charge magnitude; the electron charge is −e.
A retarding potential removes kinetic energy, with the sign convention of the electrodes stated.
limitations: No stopping endpoint for emitted electrons is supplied when emission is not allowed.
A negative energy deficit and a signed collector voltage are different quantities.

overview.text: The ideal stopping-potential magnitude is Kmax divided by the positive elementary-charge magnitude. Partial transfer or internal losses produce an inequality rather than a larger endpoint energy.

full.spoken: The positive charge magnitude times the stopping-voltage magnitude equals maximum kinetic energy, h frequency minus escape work.

full.text: \(V_s\) is a nonnegative magnitude. The sign of a laboratory electrode voltage must also specify which electrode is the reference. Using \(e\) for a positive magnitude does not change the negative charge of the electron.

If the electron receives only part of the available energy or loses energy inside matter, its outgoing kinetic energy is at most \(h\nu - \Phi\). These losses do not reverse the frequency dependence or turn extra intensity into extra energy for one electron.

An inverse energy-budget question asks for the smallest accelerating-potential magnitude capable of supplying a quantum \(h\nu\). Within that idealized conversion, \(eV\) must be at least \(h\nu\). This is an energetic lower bound, not a promise that every collision produces light.

full.returnCaption: Return to charge magnitude, signed voltage, and the retarding energy budget.

items: Choose a voltage reference and state which direction is retarding.
Keep the electron charge −e separate from the positive magnitude e.
Use Kmax/e for the positive stopping magnitude only when an emitted-electron endpoint exists.
For partial transfer or losses, replace an equality by the appropriate upper bound.
For the inverse light-production question, require at least \(h\nu\) of supplied energy before discussing conversion efficiency.

margin.text: This modern voltage-magnitude convention does not silently replace the paper’s printed charge and potential symbols. The historical 4.3-volt check belongs to its separately identified constant and unit convention in the photoelectric laboratory.
